articles.title: Trucker protest leaves supermarket shelves and gas pumps empty in southern Italy
articles.description: Trucker protest leaves supermarket shelves and gas pumps empty in southern Italy AP News Italian retailers warn of food shortages caused by truck drivers' protest Reuters Italy Buffalo Mozzarella Output Halted by Trucker Protests Bloomberg.com Italy's pasta production 'grounds to a halt' as truck drivers protest The Independent Truckers protest in southern Italy over soaring fuel prices Wanted in Rome
articles.content: MILAN (AP) — Some supermarket shelves and gas station pumps were empty in the southern city of Naples on Tuesday due to a weeklong protest by truck drivers against the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war. Protesters blocked the loading and unloading of fresh food and other goods at supermarket distribution warehouses near Naples on Monday, Sky TG24 reported. The truckers are adding their voices to demonstrations that have spread across Europe as the war disrupts economies. One supermarket in the city posted a note on empty shelves apologizing that “some products may be temporarily unavailable or available in a reduced range” due to the truckers’ strike. Shortages of fresh pasta, packaged cheeses and meats as well as produce have been reported in Sicily, partly due to stockpiling by shoppers. Partially empty supermarket shelves were also reported in the southern regions of Calabria and Puglia. A notice on empty shelves at a supermarket apologizes to customers for the lack of products, due to an ongoing truckers strike in Naples, Italy, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino) A notice on empty shelves at a supermarket apologizes to customers for the lack of products, due to an ongoing truckers strike in Naples, Italy, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. (AP Photo/Alessandra Tarantino) Transport Minister Matteo Salvini met Tuesday with national trucking associations to help the truckers cope, promising tax credits to offset soaring diesel prices and funds to modernize trucking fees. Diesel prices are roughly a third higher than before the Iran war, despite government-backed efforts to curb pump prices. A temporary diesel tax discount expired earlier this month. The president of the Unatras group of trucking associations, Paolo Uggè, said Salvini promised that payments would begin Wednesday and pledged legislation to address operating costs, the news agency LaPresse reported. Another meeting was set for next week.

articles.title: Anthropic pitches AI safety bill that may block a model if 50+ people could be killed
articles.description: The proposed policy seems to offer protections against AI running amok but actually forbids federal agencies from blocking a model's release without the permission of a judge.
articles.content: Over the past year, concerns have swirled over the potential dangers posed by artificial intelligence, and debates have raged over the proper path for AI safety. Now, Anthropic appears to have put forth its own vision for how the government might regulate its industry. Politico recently reported that the AI lab has been shopping around a new draft bill on AI safety that it hopes Congress might consider adopting. The legislation posits certain scenarios in which the release of an AI model could be blocked from distribution. Those scenarios involve a “foreseeable, imminent risk” — one in which over 50 people are at risk of dying or if over a billion dollars in property damage could result, Politico writes. The catastrophic risk in question must “stem from the creation or release of a biological weapon, the model evading its developer’s controls or a cyberattack,” the outlet notes. The metrics offered here — 50 people and a billion dollars — are similar to those in a piece of California legislation that was recently passed into law, Senate Bill 53, which similarly defined those scenarios as tantamount to “catastrophic risk.” Anthropic’s bill suggests that analysis of a model’s potential for disaster could be arrived at via the use of “independent evaluators” who would be registered with the U.S. Commerce Department. These evaluators could potentially be paid by the AI labs themselves — so long as the “payment is not contingent on the evaluations’ results,” Politico writes. It’s not clear how this proposed system would ensure that payments couldn’t influence the evaluation. Demis Hassabis, chairman of DeepMind, posited some months ago that a self-governing AI regulatory body should mimic the financial industry’s Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA). In Anthropic’s draft bill, when evaluators determine that an imminent catastrophic risk is posed, they would have 72 hours to contact the Commerce Department about it. The Commerce Department would then have to request to a Washington, D.C., judge a halt to the model’s release. The legislation would expressly forbid any federal agency from having the discretion to halt the model’s distribution on its own, Politico writes. Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment, but a spokesperson did confirm the draft bill to Politico. “This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” the spokesperson said. The theoretical risks offered in the draft policy are a little bit far afield from the kinds of incidents that have been top of mind for the tech industry of late. While there are people warning of the potential of human death, the primary concern has largely been the threat of agentic hacking. A rash of incidents in which AI programs have apparently disobeyed their human operators and hacked websites on the open internet has spurred concern that models may be lacking proper security controls. In an effort to present a solution to the spectacle of crisis that the labs themselves have helped bring about, companies like Anthropic have offered up their own preferred solutions. Indeed, despite labs’ perpetual warnings that the technology they’re selling could result in the demise of human civilization, they have largely been resistant to mandatory government oversight. Instead, they have suggested a voluntary system of embedded evaluators — supposedly “neutral” third-party observers who are placed inside AI organizations to monitor the models for potential signs of risk or abuse. Still, Anthropic’s mere suggestion for legislation appears to go slightly further than others’ regulatory proposals offered by the industry, including Nvidia, whose CEO, Jensen Huang, recently argued that the AI industry didn’t need any new laws at all. articles.title: The Millionaire Nurse
articles.description: East Lansing resident Tony Bailey is sharing financial advice in his book "The Nurse Who Beat Wall Street: How I turned my 401(k) Into $2 Million Before 50."
articles.content: Tony Bailey’s life has followed the working class Michigan archetype. He grew up in Davison, where the population has hovered between 5,000 and 6,000 for the last 50 years. His father worked for General Motors, his mother cut hair part time out of the family home, and he attended Michigan State University, studying to become a nurse. One small detail makes Bailey an outlier: He’s a millionaire. And he’s sharing his story in his new book “The Nurse Who Beat Wall Street: How I Turned My 401(k) Into $2 Million Before 50.” Bailey has lived in East Lansing for 26 years and works at University of Michigan Health-Sparrow Hospital. He also teaches nursing students at Lansing Community College. But his financial goals began long before his career goals took shape. “When I was at a young age, I set out a goal to become a millionaire by the time I retired,” he told East Lansing Info in an interview. “It just happened so much faster than I anticipated.” He credits compound interest and investing substantial amounts of money into his 401(k) early in his career. “Those early dollars worked extremely hard,” he said. “I didn’t understand or appreciate [compounding interest]. It was boring, but it was boring until it wasn’t.” The millionaire nurse is unassuming and affable, possessing both the manners and modesty associated with “Midwestern nice.” Despite his passion for investing and financial success, he is careful that his advice and story don’t come across as boastful. “I grew up working class,” he said. “I saw the work ethic in both my parents, but I didn’t grow up wealthy. But they had a dedication to their jobs and their grit helped me in my career, as well.” Bailey said that despite their shared hard work and grit, his parents differed in their approaches to money. His father was “kind of cheap” and liked to save money, investing in mutual funds. His mother, however, was “more of a spender” but never lived beyond her means. Despite his own success with saving and investing, Bailey said he never evangelized about his financial knowledge and experience. “Up until when my book came out, nobody really knew,” he said. “I didn’t tell anybody that I was a millionaire. I didn’t share my 401(k) value. But, I took care of patients and dealt with mortality. Some of them realized at the end of their life …these people had regrets that really bothered them. They had things they had accomplished, but they talked about those regrets.” Those experiences made Bailey realize he would regret not helping others, particularly nurses and working-class people, achieve financial security. And he’s already seen the impact. He said readers have told him they hadn’t looked at their retirement accounts in years, but his story helped them overcome their reluctance. “That’s what I really want,” he said. “To get people engaged and pay a little more attention to it.” Bailey said the road to financial security begins early, when someone gets their first job with the opportunity to contribute to a retirement fund or 401(k). If an employer offers matching contributions, he said it’s important to take advantage of them. As raises and pay increases come, he recommends increasing retirement contributions. “Get in the habit of investing first before you have that opportunity to spend it,” he said. “Start young and let that money work hard for you. You’re going to work hard over your career and your money should be working hard for you as well.” He smirks when asked what kind of car he drives. “A 2022 Grand Cherokee [Jeep],” he responds. “We’ve got social media that glamorizes these flashy cars and big houses and jewelry. They glamorize depreciating assets, so I stay away from the get-rich-quick things. I like long term investing and building wealth.” Bailey said he and his wife drive used vehicles, eat most of their meals at home and shop at Costco and Sam’s Club. They avoid most streaming services — “they slowly eat away” at savings — and brew their own coffee at home. “If we’re making a big purchase, we sit on it for a day or two,” he said. “There’s always good communication with my wife and myself about whether [it’s] something we need so and we’ve got to agree on that.” Bailey said he might retire at 55 because of a rule that allows individuals to access their 401(k) funds at that age without an early withdrawal penalty. “I’ve worked hard and saved and I think about enjoying [retirement] while I’m still young enough to do something,” he said. “I don’t think I’ll completely retire. I could see myself continuing to teach.” His book, “The Nurse Who Beat Wall Street,” is available at Schuler Books in Okemos and the Sparrow Hospital gift shop, as well as on Amazon. But he’s hoping the East Lansing Public Library gets a copy soon. “I know money’s tight for people,” he said. “I want them to be able to check it out without having to spend money.” Do you have a question that you would like ELi to investigate? FDA Approves First-of-Its-Kind Chronic Hepatitis B Treatment
articles.description: FDA today approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis.
articles.content: New treatment may allow some patients to maintain viral control after stopping all hepatitis B therapy The U.S. Food and Drug Administration today approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis. Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B. Hibsago is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have been taking HBV antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed levels of HBV in their blood and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less, as determined by an FDA-authorized test. “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” said Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago works by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins, helping reduce the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body. The FDA also authorized the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to aid in the selection of patients with chronic HBV infection for treatment with antiviral therapy in accordance with the FDA approved drug labeling and to assist in monitoring patients throughout the course of treatment. Researchers studied Hibsago in two clinical trials that compared it with a placebo, an inactive treatment. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. Patients take it alongside their existing hepatitis B medicine and continue that medicine for at least 24 weeks after their last Hibsago injection. Some patients may then be able to stop their existing medicine if they meet certain health and lab test requirements. Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood. Hibsago has a boxed warning for serious liver reactions as well as low platelet counts, which can increase the risk of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Hibsago also has warnings for worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, and serious risks if the injection is not administered properly. Patients need regular blood tests and follow up with their healthcare provider before and during treatment to monitor these risks. The most common side effects, excluding laboratory abnormalities, are injection site reactions, fever, fatigue and headache. The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review. The approval was granted to GSK plc. Media:FDA Request for Comment202-690-6343 The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

Mayor Mamdani Expands Community-Based Violence Prevention to Bushwick, Harlem, and Washington Heights/Inwood
articles.content: NEW YORK—Mayor Zohran Kwame Mamdani, Deputy Mayor for Community Safety Renita Francois and the Office of Community Safety today announced the expansion of New York City’s Crisis Management System (CMS) to Bushwick, Harlem and Washington Heights/Inwood. The expansion will strengthen the City’s work of credible messengers — trusted community member who work to mediate conflicts before they become violence — while connecting New Yorkers to jobs, mental health services, mentorship, education and other resources. The three neighborhoods, known as catchment areas, were selected based on crime data, unmet service needs and other indicators. Each full CMS catchment receives $1.6 million in City funding. The expansion reflects the Mamdani administration’s evidence-based, whole-of-government approach to public safety: preventing violence before it happens by investing in the people and community organizations that know their neighborhoods best. “Public safety is strongest when it begins with prevention and when communities have the resources to resolve conflict, support young people and keep their neighbors safe,” said Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “By expanding the Crisis Management System in Bushwick, Harlem and Washington Heights/Inwood, we are investing in trusted local organizations and credible messengers who know their communities and have earned their trust. That is how we build a safer New York City: by pairing accountability with opportunity and making sure every neighborhood has the resources to keep its people safe.” “Every New Yorker deserves to be safe in their neighborhood, and that safety is strongest when it is built with — not imposed on — communities,” said Deputy Mayor for Community Safety Renita Francois. “This expansion gives trusted local partners the resources they need to reach people before a crisis, interrupt violence and respond to community needs with care, credibility and urgency.” Developed through investments from the City Council and the administration more than a decade ago, the CMS is a network of community-based organizations working to prevent and reduce gun violence in neighborhoods most affected by it. CMS combines immediate conflict prevention with sustained support to help New Yorkers build safer futures. CMS partners deploy trained outreach workers and violence interrupters, often known as credible messengers, who have deep roots in their communities and are able to build trust with people at greatest risk of becoming involved in violence. Teams identify and de-escalate disputes before they turn violent, support residents after violent incidents and help prevent retaliation. They also connect participants to job training, employment, education, mental health care, legal assistance and other services. CMS currently operates across 46 neighborhood service areas. “Community safety requires sustained investment in the people and organizations best positioned to prevent harm and support healing,” said Dr. Ayesha Delany-Brumsey, Commissioner of the Office of Community Safety. “By strengthening credible-messenger outreach and access to clinical support, we are helping community partners address conflict, connect New Yorkers to care and deliver more comprehensive violence-prevention services.” “Violence prevention is most effective when it is led by people who understand a neighborhood’s strengths, challenges and relationships firsthand,” said Clifford Larochel, Executive Director of the Office of Neighborhood Safety in the Mayor’s Office of Community Safety. “This investment will help credible messengers deepen their presence and connect more New Yorkers to support before a crisis escalates.” “Public safety is about trust, which must be built in close partnership with our communities,” said Public Advocate Jumaane D. Williams. “This investment empowers trusted organizations with existing roots in our neighborhoods to continue their lifesaving work of prevention, mediation and outreach. As one of the people who helped bring the Crisis Management System to our city years ago, I’m eager to reach more New Yorkers with a proven solution to violence that puts community at its center.” “Across Brooklyn we’ve seen that the people who live in our neighborhoods are the ones best positioned to mediate conflict, support families and connect neighbors to opportunity. It’s great to see the City investing in this approach and recognizing that public safety must be built with communities, not imposed on them,” said Brooklyn Borough President Antonio Reynoso. “I’m grateful to Mayor Mamdani and Deputy Mayor Francois for expanding the Crisis Management System to Bushwick, and excited to see The Wick Against Violence expand their outreach in the neighborhood.” “Real public safety is not achieved through enforcement alone—it requires prevention, opportunity, and sustained investment in the communities most affected by violence. For years, I have proudly supported The Wick Against Violence because its work demonstrates that when we invest in trusted community organizations and credible messengers, we can interrupt violence before it happens, reach young people before they are drawn into it, and give families a path toward stability and hope. We cannot simply react to violence after lives have been lost; we must confront its root causes and invest in the people who can prevent it. I commend Mayor Mamdani for expanding the Crisis Management System into Bushwick and across the city strengthening a community-driven approach that makes our neighborhoods safer by building trust, creating opportunity, and protecting lives,” said Congresswoman Nydia Velazquez. “Violence interrupters are an essential component of crime reduction and my office’s partnership with them is part of the reason gun violence in Brooklyn is decreasing faster than the record-breaking numbers citywide. I’m very familiar with the great work Wick Against Violence is already doing in Bushwick and I know the importance of having credible messengers from the community, especially in this predominantly Latino neighborhood. CMS sites are effective and expanding them is the correct approach, so I commend Mayor Mamdani for his investment in community-led public safety,” Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez. “I applaud the Mamdani administration for expanding this important public safety initiative. Credible messengers are a proven way to interrupt and prevent violence and have been a key pillar of my office’s strategy to drive down shootings. The Crisis Management System is illustrative of the comprehensive approach we need to create lasting safety in all our communities, and I look forward to seeing the progress of the program in these new precincts,” said District Attorney Bragg. “The Wick Against Violence has already had such a valuable impact in our community, and I’m so glad to see the city expanding its operations and programming as part of the Crisis Management System. This means more people in Bushwick that are at risk of gun violence will be able to access the support they need from the messengers and organizations they trust,” said State Senator Julia Salazar. “Expanding New York City’s Crisis Management System into Bushwick is a key step toward building safer communities through prevention, intervention and support. We know that community-based violence interrupters and trusted messengers can really make a difference in preventing shootings. As we welcome The Wick and Southside United Los Sures to this effort, we need to provide them the resources, timely funding and support they need to succeed. Investing in our communities and addressing the root causes of violence are essential to creating a safer Bushwick and a safer New York City,” said Assemblywoman Maritza Davila. “Mayor Mamdani’s investment in Bushwick Houses through community-based program ‘The Wick Against Violence’ is a testament to a deeply thoughtful and comprehensive approach to improving public safety” said Council Member Jennifer Gutiérrez, who represents the development. “'The Wick’, along with partners like Woodhull Hospital H&H, the Bushwick Houses Tenants Association and Southside United HDFC, have made remarkable strides in empowering our youth, employing local residents and reducing crime. Since its MAP designation close to ten years ago, our district has witnessed the improvements made when we invest in public housing and our community. I applaud the administration’s decision to increase their investment into my district and look forward to continued success of ’The Wick Against Violence.” “Public safety is not just relying on police response to solve deeply systemic issues — it’s about preventing violence before it even happens,” said Council Member Carmen De La Rosa, representing Washington Heights & Inwood. “Investing in Grow Up Grow Out is an investment in the safety and future of Washington Heights and Inwood. By expanding trusted street outreach, mentorship, and violence intervention, we are empowering community leaders who know our young people and understand their challenges. We applaud the expansion of the credible messengers program, relying on organizations who have built the community trust to be able to intervene before conflict turns into tragedy.” “Lasting safety starts with prevention. Expanding the Crisis Management System into Harlem puts more credible messengers in our neighborhoods to resolve conflicts before they escalate, support families after a crisis and connect young people to mentorship, jobs, education and mental health care. Living Redemption is already doing this work, and this investment will help them reach more people. Thank you to Mayor Mamdani and Deputy Mayor Francois for this commitment,” said Council Member Yusef Salaam. In Bushwick, the City will expand The Wick Against Violence, operated by Southside United, to strengthen neighborhood outreach and support residents at risk of gun violence. The investment builds on Southside United’s existing work at Woodhull Hospital and programming at Bushwick Houses, giving the organization additional resources to deepen neighborhood outreach and provide sustained support to residents at risk of gun violence. The new investment will expand Living Redemption’s neighborhood outreach and conflict-mediation work, while connecting more young people and families with trusted mentors and pathways to employment, education and other support. In Washington Heights/Inwood, the City will establish a new CMS street-outreach team through Grow Up Grow Out Jr., operated by United Way, bringing CMS outreach services to an area the network has not previously covered. Trained neighborhood workers will provide street outreach, conflict mediation and ongoing support to residents at risk of becoming involved in violence.

articles.title: FDA Approves Once-Weekly Generic Hormone Therapy Patch for Women
articles.description: Today, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved the first generic of Climara Pro (estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system, 0.045 mg per day/0.015 mg), a transdermal hormone therapy patch for women with an intact uterus applied once a week.
articles.content: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration yesterday approved the first generic of Climara Pro (estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system, 0.045 mg per day/0.015 mg), a transdermal hormone therapy patch for women with an intact uterus applied once a week. The approval aligns with FDA’s Public Health Pillar: Increasing Access to Affordable Medicines & Medical Products. “Menopause is a universal experience for women, and it can greatly affect a person’s quality of life. This approval makes effective treatment more accessible,” said Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, J.D. “Approvals like this reflect FDA’s ongoing commitment to expanding American patient access to safe, affordable, high-quality medications.” The generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system is therapeutically equivalent to Climara Pro, which is indicated for use in women with an intact uterus for: Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system contain both estrogen and progestogen in a single patch; this differs from estrogen-only patches commonly used in menopause treatment. Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are specifically approved for women with an intact uterus, as the progestogen component is included to reduce the risk of endometrial hyperplasia that can occur with estrogen use alone. “Once-weekly dosing can make a real difference in how patients manage their care,” said Michael Davis, M.D., Ph.D., Director of FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “A patch offers a convenient alternative to daily oral medications, which may help patients stay on track with their treatment.” Climara Pro and the generic estradiol and levonorgestrel transdermal system are contraindicated in patients with undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding; breast cancer or a history of breast cancer; estrogen-dependent neoplasia; active deep vein thrombosis (DVT), pulmonary embolism (PE) or a history of these conditions; active arterial thromboembolic disease or a history of these conditions; known anaphylactic reaction or angioedema or hypersensitivity to estradiol and levonorgestrel; hepatic impairment or disease; and protein C, protein S, or antithrombin deficiency, or other thrombophilic disorders. The most common adverse reactions (greater than or equal to 5%) are: application site reaction, vaginal bleeding, breast pain, upper respiratory infection, back pain, depression, pain, headache and flu syndrome. In the U.S., nine out of 10 prescriptions filled are for generic drugs. Increasing the availability of generic drugs helps to create competition in the marketplace, which then helps to make treatment more affordable and increases access to healthcare for more patients. Learn more about the FDA Drug Competition Action Plan. Climara Pro is a registered trademark of Bayer. The FDA approved Zydus Pharmaceuticals (USA) Inc.’s Estradiol and Levonorgestrel Transdermal System. Please contact the manufacturer for information about the medicine’s availability. Media:FDA Request for Comment202-690-6343 The FDA, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, protects the public health by assuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of human and veterinary drugs, vaccines and other biological products for human use, and medical devices. The agency also is responsible for the safety and security of our nation’s food supply, cosmetics, dietary supplements, radiation-emitting electronic products, and for regulating tobacco products.

Why Mamdani opposes RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's NYC event
articles.content: Zohran Mamdani called the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" ahead of Mohan Bhagwat's New York event. But can the mayor do anything to stop it? New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it. Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK. When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event." Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from." His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India." "It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision." The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity. However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled. "Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity." The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS, is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance. The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, days earlier, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged sanctions against the RSS and asked the American government not to extend diplomatic courtesies to RSS members. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims." United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more. India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities. The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi.
